name: Baker County
intro: Experience the historic communities, open landscapes and mountain scenery of northeastern Oregon.
area: Approximately 3,088 square miles, including 3,068 square miles of land and 20 square miles of water.
population: 16,658, based on the U.S. Census Bureau’s July 1, 2025 population estimate.
contentHtml:
About Baker County

Located in northeastern Oregon, Baker County is known for its wide valleys, rugged mountains, high-desert terrain and historic rural communities. Baker City serves as the county seat and the primary center for commerce, culture and visitor services.

The county’s landscape stretches from the Elkhorn Mountains and forested recreation areas in the west to the Snake River country along Oregon’s eastern border. Ranchlands, agricultural fields, mountain lakes and scenic highways contribute to the area’s distinctive character.

Baker County also has deep connections to the Oregon Trail, gold mining, ranching, timber production and railroad development. These influences continue to shape the county’s architecture, communities and regional identity.

History of Baker County

Baker County was created on September 22, 1862, from a portion of Wasco County. It was named in honor of Edward Dickinson Baker, an Oregon senator and Civil War colonel who was killed during the Battle of Ball’s Bluff in 1861.

The mining settlement of Auburn originally served as the county seat. Gold discoveries in the region brought miners, merchants and settlers to eastern Oregon, and Auburn briefly became one of the area’s most active communities. As mining declined and Baker City developed into a larger commercial center, county voters selected Baker City as the permanent county seat in 1868.

During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, railroad expansion supported the growth of mining, timber, agriculture and livestock operations. Communities such as Baker City and Sumpter developed around these industries and became important centers of activity in northeastern Oregon.

Today, Baker County preserves its heritage through its historic buildings, rural communities, mining-era landmarks and connections to the Oregon Trail. Agriculture, forestry, tourism and outdoor recreation remain important parts of the county’s economy and identity.

name: Benton County
intro: Explore the rivers, forests, farmland and welcoming communities of Oregon’s central Willamette Valley.
population: 97,728, based on the U.S. Census Bureau’s July 1, 2025 estimate
contentHtml:
About Benton County

Located in western Oregon, Benton County brings together the fertile landscapes of the Willamette Valley and the forested slopes of the Oregon Coast Range. The Willamette River forms much of the county’s eastern boundary, while Marys Peak and the surrounding mountains shape its western landscape.

Corvallis serves as the county seat and the primary center for education, commerce and community life. Beyond the city, Benton County includes smaller communities, agricultural lands, rivers, wetlands, forests and scenic rural roads.

The county is known for its balance of natural surroundings, productive farmland and educational and cultural activity. Its landscape supports farming, forestry, research, conservation and outdoor recreation, while its communities preserve a strong connection to local history and the environment.

History of Benton County

Benton County was created on December 23, 1847, by the Provisional Government of Oregon. It was named in honor of Thomas Hart Benton, a United States senator from Missouri who supported westward expansion and American control of the Oregon Country.

When originally established, Benton County was much larger than it is today. Its territory included land west of the Willamette River and south of Polk County, extending to the California border and the Pacific Ocean. Portions of the original county were later used to form Coos, Curry, Douglas, Jackson, Josephine, Lane and Lincoln counties, leaving Benton County with its present boundaries.

The region has a much longer Indigenous history, particularly through the Kalapuya people and other Native communities connected to the Willamette Valley. The county’s official history records that Indigenous land claims within the area were ceded under the Treaty of Dayton in 1855.

Corvallis, originally known as Marysville, became the county seat in 1851. The community developed along the Willamette River as settlers arrived, agricultural production expanded and river transportation connected the area with other parts of Oregon. The city was renamed Corvallis and was incorporated in 1857.

Agriculture, timber production, river transportation and education played important roles in the county’s later growth. Corvallis College was designated Oregon’s land-grant institution in 1868 and eventually became Oregon State University, helping establish education and research as lasting parts of the county’s identity.

Today, Benton County combines its agricultural and rural heritage with education, environmental research, conservation and community development.

name: Clackamas County
intro: Explore historic riverfront communities, fertile farmland, forested waterways and the mountain landscapes surrounding Mount Hood.
population: 426,280, based on the U.S. Census Bureau’s July 1, 2025 population estimate
contentHtml:
About Clackamas County

Located in northwestern Oregon, Clackamas County is one of the state’s most geographically diverse counties. Its landscape includes established cities and suburban communities in the north, agricultural valleys and rural towns in the west and south, and forests, rivers and mountain terrain in the east.

Oregon City serves as the county seat and remains an important historical and cultural center. Other communities throughout the county contribute to a varied regional character that combines urban services, small-town life, agricultural traditions and access to natural surroundings.

The Willamette, Clackamas, Molalla and Sandy rivers have shaped the county’s communities, economy and environment. Farmland, forestland, lakes and mountain areas support agriculture, forestry, tourism and year-round outdoor recreation.

Clackamas County stretches from communities near Happy Valley and Wilsonville to Government Camp and the Mount Hood National Forest. This range of landscapes gives the county a distinctive combination of city life, rural countryside and protected natural areas.

History of Clackamas County

The lands now known as Clackamas County have been home to Indigenous communities for thousands of years. The Clackamas people lived in villages along the lower Willamette and Clackamas rivers and maintained an important fishing and trading center at Willamette Falls. The Molalla people lived in the foothills and highlands near the Clackamas River and the Cascade Mountains.

Clackamas County was formed on July 5, 1843, as one of the four original districts of the Oregon Country. Its original boundaries were much larger than they are today and included territory that later became part of several states and a Canadian province. By 1854, the county had assumed boundaries similar to those it has today.

Oregon City developed beside Willamette Falls and became the county seat. It was incorporated in 1844 and is recognized as the first incorporated city west of the Rocky Mountains. The city became an important destination for emigrants arriving through the Oregon Trail and the Barlow Road.

The Barlow Road opened as a regular wagon route in 1846. It allowed emigrants to travel around the southern side of Mount Hood and continue into the Willamette Valley, with many travelers eventually reaching Oregon City.

During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the rivers and forests of Clackamas County supported agriculture, timber production, transportation and manufacturing. Willamette Falls provided waterpower for early flour, woolen and paper mills and later became associated with hydroelectric development.

Today, Clackamas County preserves its Indigenous heritage, Oregon Trail history, historic communities and rural traditions while also serving as an important part of the greater Portland metropolitan region.

name: Clatsop County
intro: Discover the Pacific shoreline, Columbia River landscapes, forested headlands and historic communities of Oregon’s northern coast.
contentHtml:
About Clatsop County

Clatsop County occupies Oregon’s northwestern corner, where the Columbia River meets the Pacific Ocean. Its landscape includes broad beaches, coastal forests, river estuaries, dunes and the northern Oregon Coast Range. Astoria serves as the county seat and is the region’s main historic, cultural and commercial center.

The county’s communities are closely connected to fishing, maritime trade, forest resources and coastal tourism. The Columbia River, Pacific coastline and forested interior create a strong sense of place and provide a varied setting for outdoor recreation, wildlife viewing and scenic travel.

History of Clatsop County

The Clatsop people lived along the lower Columbia River and Pacific coast long before European and American settlement. The county was created in 1844 from the northern and western portions of the original Twality District and was named for the Clatsop Tribe.

The Lewis and Clark Expedition spent the winter of 1805 to 1806 at Fort Clatsop. Astoria was established as a fur-trading post in 1811 and became Oregon’s oldest permanent non-Indigenous settlement. Fishing, shipping, timber and tourism later became central to the county’s growth and identity.

name: Columbia County
intro: Explore Columbia River communities, wooded hills, working farms and quiet landscapes northwest of Portland.
contentHtml:
About Columbia County

Columbia County stretches along the lower Columbia River in northwestern Oregon. St. Helens serves as the county seat, while smaller riverfront and inland communities contribute to the county’s mix of rural, industrial and residential character.

The county includes forested Coast Range foothills, agricultural valleys, wetlands and long views across the Columbia River. Its economy and community life have historically been shaped by timber, manufacturing, river transportation, agriculture and access to the Portland metropolitan area.

History of Columbia County

Columbia County was created in 1854 from the northern portion of Washington County and was named for the Columbia River. The river served as the county’s most important early transportation corridor and supported trade, fishing and settlement.

Logging, sawmills and river-based industries influenced development throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Communities such as St. Helens, Scappoose, Rainier and Clatskanie grew around ports, farms, rail connections and forest resources.

name: Coos County
intro: Experience dramatic beaches, forested river valleys, coastal dunes and historic communities on Oregon’s southern coast.
contentHtml:
About Coos County

Coos County is located on Oregon’s south-central coast and includes ocean beaches, bays, estuaries, rivers, dunes and heavily forested uplands. Coquille is the county seat, while the Coos Bay area is the county’s largest population and commercial center.

The county’s natural setting supports fishing, forestry, agriculture, port activity and tourism. Coastal communities, working waterfronts and rural river valleys give Coos County a character that is closely tied to the Pacific Ocean and the forests of southwestern Oregon.

History of Coos County

The Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw peoples have longstanding connections to the region. Coos County was formed in 1853 from portions of Umpqua and Jackson counties and was named for the Coos people.

Early non-Indigenous settlement developed around Empire City and Coos Bay, where ports and timber resources supported shipping and industry. The county seat was moved from Empire City to Coquille in 1896. Timber, fishing, dairy farming and maritime trade remained important throughout the county’s later development.

name: Crook County
intro: Discover high-desert scenery, the Ochoco Mountains, winding rivers and the historic heart of Central Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Crook County

Crook County lies in Central Oregon and combines high-desert plateaus, river canyons, ranchlands and the forested Ochoco Mountains. Prineville, Oregon’s oldest incorporated city east of the Cascade Mountains, serves as the county seat.

The Crooked River and Ochoco Creek shape the county’s central valleys, while public lands provide broad views and access to forests, reservoirs and geological formations. Ranching, forestry, manufacturing, technology infrastructure and recreation all contribute to the modern economy.

History of Crook County

Crook County was created in 1882 from the southern portion of Wasco County and was named for U.S. Army officer George Crook. Prineville developed as a supply and service center for ranchers, miners and travelers in Central Oregon.

Livestock, timber and irrigated agriculture shaped early settlement. The creation of Deschutes and Jefferson counties later reduced Crook County’s original boundaries. The county has retained a strong ranching heritage while adapting to newer industries and regional growth.

name: Curry County
intro: Explore wild Pacific beaches, rugged headlands, clear rivers and dense forests along Oregon’s far southern coast.
contentHtml:
About Curry County

Curry County occupies Oregon’s southwestern corner along the Pacific Ocean and California border. Gold Beach is the county seat. The county is known for a rugged coastline, steep forested mountains, scenic river corridors and a relatively mild coastal climate.

The Rogue, Chetco and Winchuck rivers flow through the county toward the ocean. Fishing, forestry, tourism, agriculture and small coastal communities remain important to local life. Large areas of public land preserve the county’s remote and natural character.

History of Curry County

Curry County was created from the southern portion of Coos County in 1855 and was named for Oregon Territorial Governor George Law Curry. Gold discoveries and maritime access encouraged early non-Indigenous settlement, although the region’s steep terrain made travel difficult.

Mining, commercial fishing, timber harvesting and port activity supported the county’s early economy. Over time, scenic travel, outdoor recreation and retirement communities became increasingly significant, while the county retained its rural and coastal identity.

name: Deschutes County
intro: Experience Cascade peaks, volcanic landscapes, high-desert forests and vibrant communities in Central Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Deschutes County

Deschutes County is located in Central Oregon on the eastern side of the Cascade Range. Bend serves as the county seat and regional center. The county includes high-desert plateaus, pine forests, volcanic formations, rivers, lakes and views of prominent Cascade peaks.

The Deschutes River runs through the county and has influenced settlement, irrigation and recreation. Tourism, health care, construction, technology, education and outdoor industries now complement the county’s historic ties to forestry and agriculture.

History of Deschutes County

Deschutes County was created from the southern portion of Crook County in 1916. Its name comes from the Deschutes River, which French-speaking fur traders called the River of the Falls.

Irrigation projects, railroad construction and the timber industry encouraged rapid growth during the early twentieth century. Bend developed as a major lumber center before the economy diversified. The county later became one of Oregon’s fastest-growing regions, known for recreation and high-desert living.

name: Douglas County
intro: Discover the Umpqua River country, forested mountains, fertile valleys and a scenic stretch of the southern Oregon coast.
contentHtml:
About Douglas County

Douglas County extends from the Pacific Ocean across the Coast Range and Umpqua River Basin to the Cascade Mountains. Roseburg is the county seat and principal service center. The county’s large size creates a varied landscape of river valleys, forests, farms, mountains and coastline.

The North and South Umpqua rivers join near Roseburg and form one of the region’s defining natural systems. Forestry, agriculture, wine production, manufacturing, recreation and tourism contribute to the county’s economy and rural character.

History of Douglas County

Douglas County was created in 1852 from the eastern portion of the former Umpqua County and was named for U.S. Senator Stephen A. Douglas. Its boundaries changed several times as neighboring counties were organized.

The Umpqua River system supported Indigenous communities, later settlement and transportation. Gold discoveries, agriculture and timber drew newcomers during the nineteenth century. Railroads and sawmills helped Roseburg and other communities grow into commercial centers for southwestern Oregon.

name: Gilliam County
intro: Explore open wheat country, basalt canyons, the John Day River and broad Columbia Plateau skies.
contentHtml:
About Gilliam County

Gilliam County lies in north-central Oregon between the Columbia River and the interior Columbia Plateau. Condon serves as the county seat. The county is characterized by rolling wheat fields, dry grasslands, wind-swept ridges and deep river canyons.

The Columbia and John Day rivers define important parts of the county’s landscape. Agriculture, wind energy, transportation, recreation and environmental services support the local economy. Small communities and expansive views give the county a distinctly rural character.

History of Gilliam County

Gilliam County was established in 1885 from the eastern portion of Wasco County and was named for Oregon pioneer and military officer Cornelius Gilliam. Arlington, then known as Alkali, was the first county seat before voters selected Condon in 1890.

Dryland wheat farming and livestock became the foundation of the county’s economy. Rail and river transportation connected farms to regional markets, while modern wind-power development added a new use to the county’s open plateau landscape.

name: Grant County
intro: Experience mountain wilderness, river valleys, fossil landscapes and the gold-mining history of eastern Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Grant County

Grant County is located in eastern Oregon and includes the Strawberry Mountains, Blue Mountains, high-desert valleys and the headwaters of the John Day River. Canyon City is the county seat, while John Day is the largest community and a regional service center.

Large areas of public forest and rangeland shape the county’s scenery and economy. Forestry, livestock, agriculture, government services and recreation remain important. The county is also known for fossil resources, historic mining communities and remote river landscapes.

History of Grant County

Grant County was created in 1864 from portions of Wasco and Umatilla counties and was named for Ulysses S. Grant. Gold discoveries near Canyon City in 1862 brought a rapid influx of miners and merchants.

As mining declined, ranching, agriculture and timber became more important. The county’s history also includes Chinese immigrant communities, military routes and changing relationships between settlers and Indigenous peoples. Historic buildings and landscapes continue to reflect this layered past.

name: Harney County
intro: Discover vast high-desert basins, Steens Mountain, wetlands and some of Oregon’s widest open spaces.
contentHtml:
About Harney County

Harney County covers a large portion of southeastern Oregon and is the state’s largest county by area. Burns serves as the county seat. The landscape includes high-desert basins, sagebrush plains, volcanic uplands, wetlands and the dramatic fault-block profile of Steens Mountain.

The county’s open range supports cattle ranching and wildlife habitat. The Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, Alvord Desert and remote lakes draw visitors interested in birding, geology, dark skies and backcountry travel. Burns and Hines provide the county’s main community services.

History of Harney County

Harney County was created from the southern portion of Grant County in 1889 and was named for U.S. Army officer William S. Harney. The region has long been home to Northern Paiute people, whose descendants include the Burns Paiute Tribe.

Ranching, military roads, stage routes and later rail connections influenced settlement. Livestock and timber became major economic activities, while federal land management and wildlife conservation also played a large role in the county’s modern history.

name: Hood River County
intro: Explore orchard valleys, Columbia Gorge cliffs, river views and the northern slopes of Mount Hood.
contentHtml:
About Hood River County

Hood River County lies in the Columbia River Gorge and extends south toward Mount Hood. The city of Hood River is the county seat. The county includes steep forested slopes, fertile orchard land, riverfront communities and high mountain terrain.

The Hood River Valley is known for pears, apples, cherries and other fruit crops. The Columbia River supports transportation and wind sports, while mountain areas provide year-round recreation. Agriculture, tourism, health care and small industries form the modern economy.

History of Hood River County

Hood River County was created from the northwestern portion of Wasco County in 1908 through a statewide initiative. It was named for the Hood River, which flows from Mount Hood to the Columbia River.

Fruit growing became a defining industry as irrigation and transportation improved. Columbia River navigation, railroads and highways connected the valley to larger markets. The county later gained international recognition for scenic travel, wind sports and mountain recreation.

name: Jackson County
intro: Discover the Rogue Valley, historic towns, vineyards, mountain scenery and the cultural heart of southern Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Jackson County

Jackson County is located in southern Oregon and includes the Rogue Valley, Cascade and Siskiyou mountain landscapes, forests, lakes and agricultural land. Medford serves as the county seat and largest commercial center.

The county’s climate supports orchards, vineyards and diverse farming. Health care, retail, manufacturing, tourism, education and arts are also important. Communities such as Ashland, Jacksonville, Central Point and Eagle Point contribute distinct cultural and historic identities.

History of Jackson County

Jackson County was formed in 1852 from parts of Lane County and unorganized territory to the south. It was named for President Andrew Jackson. Gold discoveries near Jacksonville encouraged rapid non-Indigenous settlement during the early 1850s.

Roads and later rail connections linked the Rogue Valley with California and northern Oregon. Agriculture, timber and mining shaped early development, while Medford grew into the county’s principal transportation and commercial center. Arts, education and wine production later became major parts of the region’s identity.

name: Jefferson County
intro: Explore Central Oregon’s high-desert plateaus, river canyons, agricultural valleys and Cascade Mountain views.
contentHtml:
About Jefferson County

Jefferson County lies in Central Oregon between the Cascade Range and the high desert. Madras is the county seat. The county includes broad agricultural areas, volcanic plateaus, river canyons and views of Mount Jefferson and other Cascade peaks.

A significant part of the county lies within the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs Reservation. Agriculture, tribal enterprises, government services, tourism and outdoor recreation contribute to the local economy. The Deschutes and Crooked rivers are major landscape features.

History of Jefferson County

Jefferson County was created from the northern portion of Crook County in 1914 and was named for Mount Jefferson. The region has longstanding cultural and economic importance to the Wasco, Warm Springs and Paiute peoples.

Irrigation and dryland farming encouraged settlement around Madras and Culver. Rail transportation and highway development connected the area with regional markets. The county’s history continues to be shaped by tribal sovereignty, agriculture and access to public lands.

name: Josephine County
intro: Experience the Rogue and Illinois river valleys, forested mountains and the historic communities of southwestern Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Josephine County

Josephine County is located in southwestern Oregon along the California border. Grants Pass serves as the county seat and primary commercial center. The county includes the Rogue and Illinois river valleys, forested mountains, rural communities and extensive public lands.

The climate supports agriculture, vineyards and gardens, while rivers and forests support tourism and recreation. Health care, retail, manufacturing and services complement the county’s historic ties to mining, timber and transportation.

History of Josephine County

Josephine County was created from the western portion of Jackson County in 1856. It was named for Virginia Josephine Rollins, associated with early gold mining activity in the region.

Mining camps and supply communities developed during the mid-nineteenth century. The county seat moved from Kerby to Grants Pass as transportation routes and rail connections shifted commercial activity. Timber, agriculture and river tourism later became important parts of the local economy.

name: Klamath County
intro: Explore high-elevation lakes, volcanic landscapes, wildlife-rich wetlands and the southern Cascade region.
contentHtml:
About Klamath County

Klamath County occupies a large area of south-central Oregon. Klamath Falls is the county seat. The county includes high plateaus, forested mountains, volcanic terrain, marshes and major lakes within the Klamath Basin.

Agriculture, forestry, health care, government services, energy and tourism support the economy. The basin is nationally significant for migratory birds and wetland habitat. Parts of the county also provide access to the landscapes surrounding Crater Lake and the southern Cascades.

History of Klamath County

Klamath County was created from the western portion of Lake County in 1882 and was named for the Klamath people. The region is the homeland of the Klamath, Modoc and Yahooskin peoples, represented today by the Klamath Tribes.

Irrigation projects, railroads and timber mills encouraged twentieth-century growth in Klamath Falls and surrounding communities. Agriculture and water management became central to the regional economy and remain closely connected to tribal rights, wildlife habitat and environmental policy.

name: Lake County
intro: Discover high-desert lakes, wide valleys, forested mountains and remote communities in south-central Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Lake County

Lake County covers a broad area of south-central Oregon along the California and Nevada borders. Lakeview serves as the county seat. The landscape includes high-desert basins, alkali lakes, forested mountains, sagebrush plains and the Warner Mountains.

Ranching, forestry, agriculture, renewable energy and government services are important to the local economy. The county’s remote setting also supports dark-sky viewing, birding, geology and backcountry recreation.

History of Lake County

Lake County was created in 1874 from portions of Jackson and Wasco counties. Its name reflects the many lakes and seasonal water bodies found across the region.

Indigenous peoples maintained longstanding connections to the basin and mountain landscapes. Ranching, stage routes, timber and irrigation shaped later settlement. Lakeview developed as the county’s service and government center, while small communities remained closely tied to agriculture and public lands.

name: Lane County
intro: Travel from Pacific beaches through fertile valleys and forested rivers to the high peaks of the Cascade Range.
contentHtml:
About Lane County

Lane County extends from the Oregon coast to the Cascade Mountains and includes a wide range of landscapes. Eugene is the county seat and largest city. The county includes coastal dunes, river valleys, farmland, forests, waterfalls, mountain lakes and high-elevation wilderness.

The Willamette, McKenzie and Siuslaw river systems shape the county’s geography. Education, health care, technology, manufacturing, forestry, agriculture and tourism contribute to a diverse economy. Eugene and Springfield form the main urban area, while many smaller communities retain rural and coastal identities.

History of Lane County

Lane County was created in 1851 from portions of Linn and Benton counties and was named for Joseph Lane, the first governor of Oregon Territory. Eugene developed near the Willamette River and became the county seat.

Agriculture and river travel supported early communities. Timber and railroads later drove growth, while the University of Oregon strengthened Eugene’s role as an educational and cultural center. The county’s coastal and mountain communities developed around fishing, forestry, tourism and recreation.

name: Lincoln County
intro: Explore central Oregon’s rocky coastline, working harbors, forested headlands and river estuaries.
contentHtml:
About Lincoln County

Lincoln County occupies a scenic section of Oregon’s central coast. Newport is the county seat and largest city. The county includes ocean beaches, rocky headlands, bays, estuaries, coastal forests and the western slopes of the Coast Range.

Fishing, marine research, tourism, forestry and service industries shape the local economy. Coastal communities such as Lincoln City, Depoe Bay, Newport, Toledo, Waldport and Yachats each contribute a distinct waterfront or small-town character.

History of Lincoln County

Lincoln County was created in 1893 from western portions of Benton and Polk counties and was named for President Abraham Lincoln. Newport became the county seat and developed as a port, fishing center and coastal destination.

The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians have deep cultural ties to the region and maintain their tribal headquarters in the county. Timber, fishing, transportation and tourism influenced later growth, while marine science became an increasingly important part of Newport’s identity.

name: Linn County
intro: Discover productive Willamette Valley farmland, historic communities, river corridors and Cascade Mountain scenery.
contentHtml:
About Linn County

Linn County extends from the central Willamette Valley eastward into the Cascade Mountains. Albany is the county seat. The county includes fertile farmland, forested foothills, rivers, reservoirs, mountain passes and rural communities.

Agriculture, food processing, manufacturing, forestry, health care and education contribute to the economy. The Willamette, Santiam and Calapooia rivers influence settlement and farming, while the eastern county provides access to lakes, forests and mountain recreation.

History of Linn County

Linn County was created in 1847 from the southern portion of Champoeg County and was named for U.S. Senator Lewis F. Linn, an advocate for American settlement in Oregon.

Early communities developed along rivers and wagon routes in the Willamette Valley. Albany became a transportation, agricultural and manufacturing center. Railroads, timber processing and diversified farming later supported growth throughout the county.

name: Malheur County
intro: Explore high-desert canyons, irrigated farmland, Oregon Trail history and the wide-open landscapes of far eastern Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Malheur County

Malheur County occupies Oregon’s southeastern corner along the Idaho and Nevada borders. Vale is the county seat, while Ontario is the largest city and main commercial center. The county includes high-desert plateaus, river canyons, sagebrush range and irrigated agricultural valleys.

The Snake, Owyhee and Malheur rivers shape the landscape and support farming. Agriculture, food processing, transportation, government services and energy are major parts of the economy. The county’s location connects Oregon with markets and communities in southwestern Idaho.

History of Malheur County

Malheur County was created from the southern portion of Baker County in 1887. It was named for the Malheur River, whose French name means misfortune or bad luck.

The area includes important routes associated with the Oregon Trail and later stage and rail transportation. Irrigation transformed parts of the Snake River Plain into productive farmland. Ranching, agriculture and cross-border trade continue to shape the county’s identity.

name: Marion County
intro: Explore Oregon’s capital region, fertile farm country, river landscapes and the western slopes of the Cascades.
contentHtml:
About Marion County

Marion County lies in the central Willamette Valley and extends east into the Cascade foothills. Salem, Oregon’s capital, is the county seat and largest city. The county combines urban neighborhoods, historic towns, farmland, vineyards, forests and river valleys.

The Willamette, Santiam and Pudding rivers support agriculture and community development. State government, health care, manufacturing, education, food processing and farming are major economic sectors. The county is especially known for berries, hops, nursery crops and diverse specialty agriculture.

History of Marion County

Marion County began as Champoeg District, one of the four original districts created by Oregon’s Provisional Government in 1843. It was renamed Marion County in 1849 in honor of Revolutionary War officer Francis Marion.

The Champoeg area played a central role in the formation of Oregon’s provisional government. Salem developed as the territorial and later state capital. Agriculture, river transportation, mills and government institutions helped shape the county’s long-term growth.

name: Morrow County
intro: Discover Columbia River industry, open wheat country, rolling rangelands and the foothills of the Blue Mountains.
contentHtml:
About Morrow County

Morrow County extends from the Columbia River south into the Blue Mountain foothills. Heppner is the county seat, while Boardman and Irrigon are important communities along the Columbia River corridor.

The county’s northern area supports ports, food processing, energy and irrigated agriculture. Farther south, wheat fields, cattle ranches and rolling uplands dominate the landscape. Transportation, agriculture and energy production are central to the local economy.

History of Morrow County

Morrow County was created in 1885 from portions of Umatilla and Wasco counties. It was named for Jackson L. Morrow, a state legislator who supported the county’s formation.

Heppner developed as a ranching and trade center, while rail and river transportation connected county products to larger markets. The 1903 Heppner flood became one of Oregon’s deadliest natural disasters and remains an important part of local history. Modern growth has been strongest near the Columbia River.

name: Multnomah County
intro: Experience Oregon’s largest urban center, two major rivers, historic neighborhoods and the western Columbia River Gorge.
contentHtml:
About Multnomah County

Multnomah County is Oregon’s most populous county and its smallest by land area. Portland is the county seat and largest city. The county includes dense urban neighborhoods, industrial riverfronts, forested hills, agricultural areas on Sauvie Island and scenic landscapes in the Columbia River Gorge.

The Willamette and Columbia rivers are central to transportation, commerce and recreation. Health care, technology, education, government, manufacturing, logistics, arts and tourism support a diverse regional economy.

History of Multnomah County

Multnomah County was created in 1854 from portions of Washington and Clackamas counties. Its name is associated with the Multnomah people, a Chinookan group connected to Sauvie Island and the lower Columbia River.

Portland grew as a river port and commercial center during the nineteenth century. Railroads, bridges, manufacturing and international trade supported rapid urban expansion. The county later became Oregon’s principal center for culture, business, transportation and higher education.

name: Polk County
intro: Explore western Willamette Valley farmland, forested Coast Range foothills and welcoming historic communities.
contentHtml:
About Polk County

Polk County lies west of the Willamette River in the central Willamette Valley. Dallas is the county seat. The county includes productive farmland, vineyards, small cities, river corridors and forested areas extending into the Coast Range.

Agriculture, forestry, food production, education, government services and commuting connections to Salem support the economy. The county’s landscape shifts from valley farms in the east to wooded hills and rural communities in the west.

History of Polk County

Polk County was created from Yamhill District in 1845 and was named for President James K. Polk. Early settlement focused on the fertile valleys west of the Willamette River.

Farming, river crossings and local trade supported communities such as Dallas, Independence and Monmouth. Education became important with the development of institutions that later formed Western Oregon University. Agriculture and forestry remained central to county life.

name: Sherman County
intro: Discover sweeping wheat fields, Columbia River views and dramatic canyons in north-central Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Sherman County

Sherman County is located on the Columbia Plateau between the Deschutes and John Day rivers. Moro is the county seat. The county is known for rolling wheat fields, open ridges, dry canyons and long views toward the Columbia River and Cascade Mountains.

Dryland agriculture remains the foundation of the local economy, supported by transportation, wind energy and river access. Small communities and working farms define the county’s quiet rural character.

History of Sherman County

Sherman County was created from the northeastern portion of Wasco County in 1889 and was named for Union General William Tecumseh Sherman. Moro became the permanent county seat after an early period of competition among communities.

Wheat farming expanded as rail connections and river shipping improved access to markets. The county’s agricultural landscape has remained relatively consistent, while renewable energy and highway transportation have added newer economic activity.

name: Tillamook County
intro: Explore forested headlands, broad bays, dairy country and dramatic beaches on Oregon’s north coast.
contentHtml:
About Tillamook County

Tillamook County occupies a rugged section of Oregon’s northern coast. The city of Tillamook is the county seat. The county includes Pacific beaches, bays, estuaries, coastal forests, river valleys and productive dairy farmland.

Dairy production, forestry, fishing, tourism and small manufacturing are important to the economy. Tillamook Bay and other coastal waterways support wildlife, boating and working waterfronts, while inland valleys provide fertile pastureland.

History of Tillamook County

Tillamook County was created in 1853 from parts of Clatsop, Yamhill and Polk counties and was named for the Tillamook people. Indigenous communities maintained longstanding connections to the coast, rivers and forests.

Isolation and difficult overland travel shaped early non-Indigenous settlement. Dairy farming, timber and fishing became major industries as roads and rail connections improved. The county later became widely known for coastal tourism and agricultural products.

name: Umatilla County
intro: Discover wheat country, Blue Mountain foothills, river valleys and the cultural traditions of northeastern Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Umatilla County

Umatilla County stretches from the Columbia River south into the Blue Mountains. Pendleton serves as the county seat. The county includes broad wheat-growing plateaus, river valleys, rangelands, forests and important transportation corridors.

Agriculture, food processing, logistics, energy, manufacturing and tribal enterprises support the economy. The Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation are a major cultural and economic presence in the county.

History of Umatilla County

Umatilla County was created from the central portion of Wasco County in 1862 and was named for the Umatilla River. The region is the homeland of the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla peoples.

The Oregon Trail, military routes and river transportation encouraged nineteenth-century settlement. Pendleton became a trade and wool-processing center, while dryland wheat farming expanded across the plateau. Railroads and highways strengthened the county’s role as a transportation hub.

name: Union County
intro: Explore the Grande Ronde Valley, Blue Mountain forests, historic towns and open agricultural landscapes.
contentHtml:
About Union County

Union County is located in northeastern Oregon and is centered on the broad Grande Ronde Valley. La Grande is the county seat and largest city. The county includes fertile farmland, forested mountains, river corridors and smaller historic communities.

Agriculture, forestry, transportation, education, health care and government services support the economy. The Blue Mountains frame the valley and provide access to public lands, while Interstate 84 and rail routes connect the county with regional markets.

History of Union County

Union County was created from Baker County in 1864 and was named for the community of Union, whose name reflected support for the Union during the Civil War.

Settlement expanded in the Grande Ronde Valley because of fertile land, water and transportation routes. La Grande grew rapidly after the railroad arrived and became the county’s primary commercial center. Farming, livestock and timber remained important throughout the county’s development.

name: Wallowa County
intro: Discover alpine lakes, dramatic mountains, deep canyons and the rural communities of Oregon’s northeastern corner.
contentHtml:
About Wallowa County

Wallowa County lies in Oregon’s far northeastern corner. Enterprise is the county seat. The county includes the Wallowa Mountains, Wallowa Valley, Hells Canyon, forested river corridors and broad agricultural lands.

Agriculture, livestock, forestry, arts and tourism support the local economy. The county’s mountain scenery and small communities create a strong rural identity, while large public-land areas provide access to wilderness and rivers.

History of Wallowa County

Wallowa County was created from the eastern portion of Union County in 1887. Its name comes from a Nez Perce word associated with a fish-trap support. The Wallowa Valley is part of the homeland of the Joseph Band of the Nez Perce.

Euro-American settlement expanded during the nineteenth century, leading to conflict and the forced removal of Chief Joseph’s band. Agriculture, ranching and timber later shaped the county’s economy. Today, local history, art and outdoor tourism are important parts of its identity.

name: Wasco County
intro: Explore Columbia Gorge scenery, dry plateau country, river canyons and one of Oregon’s oldest trading communities.
contentHtml:
About Wasco County

Wasco County lies along the Columbia River in north-central Oregon. The Dalles serves as the county seat. The county extends from the Columbia Gorge and eastern Cascade slopes into dry agricultural plateaus and the Deschutes River canyon.

Agriculture, transportation, energy, technology, government services and tourism contribute to the economy. Orchards and vineyards grow near the Columbia, while wheat fields and rangelands dominate portions of the interior.

History of Wasco County

Wasco County was created in 1854 from portions of Clackamas, Lane, Linn and Marion counties and was named for the Wasco people. At its creation, it covered an enormous territory that extended across much of the inland Pacific Northwest.

The Dalles has long been an important Indigenous trading place along the Columbia River. It later became a major stop on the Oregon Trail and a center for river transportation, military activity and commerce. Successive county formations reduced Wasco County to its present boundaries.

name: Washington County
intro: Discover the Tualatin Valley’s cities, farms, vineyards, forested hills and thriving technology corridor.
contentHtml:
About Washington County

Washington County occupies much of the Tualatin Valley west of Portland. Hillsboro is the county seat. The county combines major suburban cities, technology campuses, farmland, vineyards, forested foothills and rural communities.

Technology, health care, manufacturing, education, agriculture and retail support one of Oregon’s largest and most diverse county economies. Despite substantial urban growth, the county retains productive farmland and scenic areas near the Coast Range.

History of Washington County

The county began as Twality District, one of four original districts created by Oregon’s Provisional Government in 1843. It was renamed Washington County in 1849 in honor of President George Washington.

The Tualatin Valley attracted farmers because of its fertile soil and access to water. Railroads and roads linked communities such as Hillsboro, Forest Grove and Beaverton to Portland. During the late twentieth century, technology and advanced manufacturing became leading industries.

name: Wheeler County
intro: Explore fossil-rich hills, colorful geology, quiet river valleys and remote ranch country in north-central Oregon.
contentHtml:
About Wheeler County

Wheeler County is located in north-central Oregon and is the state’s least populous county. Fossil serves as the county seat. The county includes deeply eroded river valleys, high-desert grasslands, colorful rock formations and forested uplands.

Ranching, agriculture, government services and tourism support the local economy. The John Day River and internationally significant fossil resources give the county a distinctive geological and natural identity.

History of Wheeler County

Wheeler County was created in 1899 from portions of Grant, Gilliam and Crook counties. It was named for Henry H. Wheeler, an early mail carrier and local settler.

Ranching and small agricultural communities shaped early settlement. Fossil became the county seat and remains known for accessible fossil beds. The county’s colorful geological formations and John Day River landscapes later became important tourism resources.

name: Yamhill County
intro: Explore vineyard-covered hills, fertile farmland, historic towns and the heart of Oregon wine country.
contentHtml:
About Yamhill County

Yamhill County lies in the northwestern Willamette Valley. McMinnville is the county seat. The county includes rolling hills, river valleys, vineyards, orchards, farmland, forests and historic small towns.

Agriculture, wine production, food processing, manufacturing, education and tourism support the economy. The county is widely known for vineyards and tasting rooms, but it also retains strong connections to traditional farming and rural community life.

History of Yamhill County

Yamhill was one of the four original districts created by Oregon’s Provisional Government in 1843. The name is associated with the Yamhill band of the Kalapuya people, who lived in the Willamette Valley long before non-Indigenous settlement.

Fertile land attracted farming families during the nineteenth century. McMinnville developed as a trade and educational center, while railroads connected agricultural products with regional markets. Wine production grew rapidly in the late twentieth century and became a defining modern industry.
